floors.title: The Inquisition's Wall
floors.claim: Bernard Délicieux, the friar who led protests against Carcassonne's Inquisition prison, was himself sentenced in 1319 to spend the rest of his life inside it.
floors.answer: He was sentenced in December 1319 to life in the Inquisition's prison he had fought, and died in early 1320.
floors.explanation: The Inquisition's prison at Carcassonne was called the 'Mur' (the Wall). Its harsher regime, the 'murus strictus', meant a small, dark cell, bread and water, and chains on the feet, sometimes chained to the wall. Townspeople stormed the Wall in 1303 and freed its prisoners, and the Franciscan Bernard Délicieux, the Inquisition's loudest critic, was present. In April 1306 two papal cardinals came to Carcassonne, heard forty prisoners complain of hunger, bad bedding and cruel keepers, and dismissed the jailers. The Inquisition later won. At the end of his trial on 8 December 1319, Délicieux was sentenced to life imprisonment in the inquisitorial prison of Carcassonne, and he died in early 1320.
floors.nuance: The Inquisition's prison at Carcassonne was in use from the 1200s, but its best-documented years are 1303–1320, so this floor is dated to them. Délicieux's judges waived his chains and bread-and-water diet because of his age and weak hands; Pope John XXII is reported to have overruled them. His trial began on 3 or 12 September 1319; sources differ. Lea's history dates from the 1880s but is still standard, and his description of the 'strict wall' covers inquisitorial prisons in general, not Carcassonne alone.
floors.visual: A prison building outside the walls of the walled Cité, divided into a milder 'large' wall with corridors and a 'strict' wall of small, dark, separate cells. Archaeologists reported finding its doorway and remains in gardens in front of the ramparts (2014). Its full layout is not known.

sources.author: Henry Charles Lea
sources.supports: Defines murus largus and murus strictus (smallest, darkest cells, chains on the feet, sometimes chained to the wall; bread and water) and says cardinals investigated the Carcassonne prison and eased its rigours.

sources.title: A History of the Inquisition of the Middle Ages, vol. 2 (pp. 93–94, 101)

sources.supports: Cardinals' session at Carcassonne on 16 April 1306, their visit to 40 prisoners and the dismissal of jailers, and Délicieux's sentence of 8 December 1319 to life imprisonment 'in the inquisitorial prison of Carcassonne'.

sources.supports: Reports the discovery of the prison door by Calvayrac and Baudreu, the Mur Large / Mur Strict division, the 1303 storming, and Délicieux's 1319 life sentence and death in 1320.

sources.title: Bernard Délicieux
sources.supports: Trial at Carcassonne in 1319, life sentence in solitary confinement, the waived penance overruled by John XXII, and death in early 1320.

floors.title: Louis XI's cages
floors.claim: Cardinal Jean Balue spent eleven years locked in one of Louis XI's iron cages.
floors.answer: The cages existed, but no source from Balue's lifetime puts him in one; the Catholic Encyclopedia traces the story to 16th-century Italy.
floors.explanation: The imprisonment is real. Louis XI arrested Cardinal Jean Balue for treason in 1469 and held him until 1480, when the pope secured his release. The cages were real too. Philippe de Commynes, Louis XI's own adviser, describes the king's cruel prisons of iron, or of wood plated with iron. Commynes was held in one of them for eight months, and he was confined at Loches in 1487. But no contemporary evidence puts Balue in a cage. Commynes names Balue's fellow plotter, the Bishop of Verdun, as the first man caged, for fourteen years. The Catholic Encyclopedia calls Balue's cage 'baseless' and says the story began in 16th-century Italy, and the Columbia Encyclopedia calls it 'unproved'.
floors.nuance: The verdict rests on the absence of evidence: nothing proves Balue was never caged, but no source from his lifetime says he was. Where he was held is also unclear; some accounts say Loches, others the château of Onzain near Blois. The cage shown at Loches today is a reconstruction. The cages' nickname, 'fillettes du roi' (the king's little girls), is traditional; it could not be confirmed in the sources checked for this page.
floors.visual: Commynes describes cages of iron, or of wood covered with iron plates inside and out, too small for comfort. The dimensions of any cage at Loches are not documented in the sources I checked. The cage shown in the Loches keep today is a modern reconstruction.

sources.title: Medieval Sourcebook: Philippe de Commynes, Portrait of Louis XI (from The Memoirs of Philip de Commines, trans. A. R. Scoble, vol. II, pp. 75–81)
sources.author: Philippe de Commynes; ed. Paul Halsall
sources.supports: An eyewitness says Louis XI built cages of iron and iron-plated wood, that the Bishop of Verdun was the first put in one (for fourteen years), and that Commynes himself spent eight months in one. Balue is not mentioned.

sources.title: Jean Balue
sources.supports: Balue was held captive 1469–80 (eleven years), was freed through papal intervention in 1480, and 'the baseless story of his detention in an iron cage originated in Italy in the sixteenth century.'

sources.title: Balue, Jean
sources.supports: Louis held Balue prisoner from 1469 to 1480; 'The legend that Balue was kept in an iron cage is unproved.'

sources.title: Philippe de Commines
sources.supports: In 1487 Commynes was 'confined at Loches in one of the iron cages used by Louis XI', which ties the cages to Loches.

floors.title: Dalibor's Fiddle
floors.claim: While imprisoned in the tower in 1498, the knight Dalibor of Kozojedy taught himself the violin, and crowds gathered below to hear him play.
floors.answer: Dalibor was a real prisoner, but violins didn't reach Bohemia until about a century after his execution in 1498.
floors.explanation: Dalibor of Kozojedy was real. He was the first prisoner of the new artillery tower at Prague Castle, which was built around 1496, and he was beheaded in 1498 for siding with rebellious serfs on a neighbouring estate. The violin story is legend. Prague's official tourism board points out that the first violins did not reach Bohemia until about a century after his death. The story probably grew out of a saying, 'necessity taught Dalibor to fiddle', which is often read as a grim joke about torture making a prisoner 'sing'. As a nobleman, Dalibor seems to have had a private cell with windows and a stove, and a duller stay than the tales suggest.
floors.nuance: Even the torture explanation is uncertain. A castle guide quoted by Radio Prague says the saying's origin is still unclear and notes that nobles could not legally be tortured. Writers have retold the legend in very different ways, from Jirásek to Smetana's 1868 opera 'Dalibor'.
floors.visual: A round stone artillery tower in the castle's fortifications at the end of Golden Lane. Its lower level served as a dungeon until 1781. Dalibor's own cell is described as private, with windows and a stove.

sources.title: About Daliborka (Legends of Prague)
sources.supports: Tells the legend, then says 'the first violins did not arrive in Bohemia until about a hundred years after Dalibor's execution' and that the saying likely means suffering on the rack forced him to confess.

sources.title: Daliborka: Prague Castle's medieval prison whose first inmate inspired a national legend
sources.author: Thomas McEnchroe
sources.supports: The tower was built around 1496 and Dalibor was its first prisoner, executed in 1498. As a noble he had a private cell with windows and a stove; a guide says the 'fiddle' may be a torture device but the origin is unclear.

floors.place: Veytaux, near Montreux, Lake Geneva, Switzerland
floors.title: The Prisoner of Chillon
floors.claim: François Bonivard spent all six of his years at Chillon chained to a pillar in the lakeside dungeon.
floors.answer: Bonivard spent about two years in rooms in the castle and four in the dungeon. The chained-to-a-pillar picture comes from Byron's poem.
floors.explanation: Bonivard, a Genevan prior who opposed the Duke of Savoy, really was held at Chillon from 1530 until the Bernese freed him in 1536. He was not in the dungeon the whole time. Swiss historians note that for the first two years his noble rank earned him two rooms in the castle. Only when the duke judged this too lenient was he moved underground. Bonivard himself wrote that he was thrust 'into a cell lower than the lake, where I lived four years'. The image of him chained to the fifth pillar comes from Byron's 1816 poem, which Byron subtitled 'A Fable'. Excavations found no sign of the path Bonivard said he wore into the rock floor.
floors.nuance: Accounts differ: one Chillon guide told swissinfo it was only the last six months in the dungeon, and some sources date the start of his imprisonment to 1532. Byron also invented the imprisoned brothers. The historical Bonivard had two brothers, but not as fellow prisoners.
floors.visual: A vaulted Gothic undercroft cut partly from the rock at lake level, with a row of stone columns and windows onto Lake Geneva. Byron's name is carved on one pillar.

sources.title: In the footsteps of the real prisoner of Chillon
sources.author: Olivier Pauchard
sources.supports: Captured 1530, freed 1536; first two years in two rooms in the castle, then four years underground; no trace of a prisoner found around the columns.

sources.title: The Works of Lord Byron, Poetry vol. 4: The Prisoner of Chillon (introduction and notes)
sources.author: ed. Ernest Hartley Coleridge
sources.supports: Quotes Bonivard: 'the captain thrust me into a cell lower than the lake, where I lived four years'; confinement 1530 to 1 February 1536; Byron admits he 'was not sufficiently aware of the history of Bonnivard'; the historical Bonivard had 'but two brothers'.

sources.title: The 'Prisoner of Chillon' lives on
sources.author: Dale Bechtel
sources.supports: A Chillon guide says the 'chained to the fifth pillar' detail comes from Byron and cannot be confirmed.

floors.title: Cellini's Bedsheet Rope
floors.claim: Jailed in Castel Sant'Angelo, the goldsmith Benvenuto Cellini escaped down a rope made from his bedsheets and broke his leg in the fall.
floors.answer: Cellini's own memoir describes the linen rope and the broken leg, and other accounts confirm the escape and recapture.
floors.explanation: In 1538 Cellini was imprisoned in the papal fortress, accused of stealing gems from the papal treasury. In his autobiography he describes cutting his bedsheets into strips and sewing them together. He hid the strips, worked a door off its hinges, climbed onto the roof through the latrines and lowered himself down the central keep. He tied the line to a piece of ancient tile jutting from the wall. Knocked out by a fall from the outer wall, he woke to find his 'right leg was broken three inches above the heel' and crawled into Rome on hands and knees. Independent summaries agree that he escaped with bedsheets, broke his leg and was recaptured, then later released through the Cardinal of Ferrara.
floors.nuance: The escape's details come from Cellini's own boastful memoir, though the imprisonment, escape and recapture are not in doubt. Dates vary: Symonds says Cellini was sent to prison in 1538, while the Catholic Encyclopedia gives 1537–1539. The 'rope' was strips of linen sewn together rather than knotted sheets.
floors.visual: The massive round central keep of Hadrian's former mausoleum, with several stages of high walls below it. Cellini describes climbing to the roof by the latrines and descending on a long band of linen strips rolled on two sticks.

sources.title: The Life of Benvenuto Cellini, vol. 2 (Book I, the escape, c. pp. 24–30)
sources.author: Benvenuto Cellini; trans. John Addington Symonds
sources.supports: Cellini cut sheets into strips to clear 'the great height of the central keep of Sant' Agnolo', climbed out by the latrines, fell, and found 'my right leg was broken three inches above the heel.'

sources.title: The Life of Benvenuto Cellini, vol. 1 (Symonds's introduction)

sources.supports: He escaped 'by using bedsheets to lower himself from the prison tower and over the prison walls' and, 'having broken his leg in flight, he is recaptured.'

sources.title: Benvenuto Cellini
sources.supports: Accused of stealing Church funds and imprisoned in Sant'Angelo; escaped, was recaptured and treated harshly; Cardinal Ferrara obtained his release.

floors.title: The Bottle Dungeon
floors.claim: After Cardinal David Beaton was murdered in his castle in 1546, his killers dumped his body into the castle's bottle dungeon.
floors.answer: Historic Environment Scotland says the murdered cardinal's body was certainly kept in the bottle dungeon, packed in salt.
floors.explanation: In March 1546 Cardinal Beaton had the Protestant preacher George Wishart burned outside St Andrews Castle. On 29 May 1546 a group of Fife lairds got into the castle disguised as masons and murdered the cardinal. According to Historic Environment Scotland, which cares for the castle, they hung his naked body in a pair of sheets from the castle walls, then threw it into the bottle dungeon in the Sea Tower. HES describes the dungeon as 'a dank and airless pit cut out of the solid rock'. Citing John Knox, it says the body was kept there covered in salt to 'keip him frome stinking'. HES states that the body 'was certainly kept' there.
floors.nuance: Knox's own wording refers to the Sea Tower, and how long the body lay there (weeks or months) and where it was finally buried are uncertain. The Sea Tower is the castle's north-west tower. HES says only that Wishart 'may' have been held in the dungeon.
floors.visual: A bottle-shaped pit about 22 ft (7 m) deep, cut into the rock below the Sea Tower. Its only entrance is a narrow neck at the top, opened by a trapdoor in the floor of the tower vault, so prisoners had to be lowered in.

sources.title: Statement of Significance: St Andrews Castle (PIC034)
sources.supports: Timeline for 1546: the murderers 'hang his naked body in a pair of sheets from the castle walls, before throwing it into the castle's bottle dungeon'; the dungeon is in the Sea Tower and is 'a dank and airless pit cut out of the solid rock'.

sources.title: The macabre murder of Cardinal Beaton
sources.author: Julia Morrison
sources.supports: Murder on 29 May 1546; body thrown into the 'notorious bottle dungeon'; citing Knox, kept there covered in salt to 'keip him frome stinking'.

sources.title: St Andrews Castle: Overview

sources.title: St Andrews Castle

floors.place: Old Town Hall (Altes Rathaus), Nuremberg, Franconia, Germany
floors.title: The Hole Under the Town Hall
floors.claim: Prisoners in Nuremberg's 'hole' cells beneath the town hall were usually serving long prison sentences there.
floors.answer: The cells mostly held people awaiting trial or execution. Punishment was usually branding, flogging or death, not a long sentence.
floors.explanation: The Lochgefängnisse (hole prisons) were cut from the vaults of a former bread house when Nuremberg built its town hall in the 14th century. The town hall was also the law court. The city's museums say the cells were reserved mainly for people awaiting trial and people condemned to death. They were a holding pen, not a place to serve a sentence. Prisoners sat in darkness in small wood-lined cells and paid for their own food. In a vault called the 'chapel', they could be tortured to extract confessions, by methods the city court chose. Punishments themselves were usually physical: branding, flogging or execution outside the walls. The sculptor Veit Stoss, the cells' most famous inmate, was held here for forgery and spared execution: he was branded instead.
floors.nuance: 'Usually' matters: a few people may have stayed longer, but other towers, such as the debtors' tower, served as the city's regular prisons. Most of the sources are the City of Nuremberg's own museum and tourism pages. Bavaria abolished torture by decree in 1806; its new criminal code followed in 1813.
floors.visual: A low, vaulted cellar under the Old Town Hall with a row of tiny cells about 2 × 2 m, lined with wooden planks on floor, walls and ceiling. Each held a plank bed, a bench and a board for a table, with a heating basin in winter. There was also a larger vault (the 'chapel') used for torture, plus a forge, kitchen and well room.

sources.title: Mittelalterliche Lochgefängnisse
sources.supports: The cells were 'vor allem Untersuchungsgefangenen und Todeskandidaten vorbehalten' (mainly for those awaiting trial and those facing execution); lists cells, torture chamber, forge, prison kitchen and well room.

sources.publisher: Museums of the City of Nuremberg

sources.title: Medieval Dungeons

sources.title: Lochgefängnisse

floors.title: Little Ease
floors.claim: The Tower of London had a cell called 'Little Ease', so small that a prisoner could neither stand upright nor lie down.
floors.answer: A priest was kept there for eighteen months from 1582, and Victorian historians describe it as too small to stand or lie in, though its exact place and size are uncertain.
floors.explanation: Little Ease was a real place of punishment. Bishop Challoner's 18th-century martyrology, compiled from contemporary Catholic accounts, records that the priest Stephen Rousham was sent to the Tower in 1582 and 'thrust down into that dungeon, which is called Little Ease', where he was kept for eighteen months and thirteen days. Victorian historians of the Tower describe it the same way. Thornbury's 'Old and New London', quoting an earlier writer, says it was 'so small that a prisoner could not stand erect, or even lie down at full length'. De Ros (1866) places a dark cell of that name in the vaults of the White Tower, with a heavy door and no opening for light or air.
floors.nuance: Its exact location and size are uncertain. Sources say beneath the White Tower, but no one knows for sure which space it was, and figures such as '4 feet square' are not well sourced. The tradition that Guy Fawkes was held there in 1605 is unproven, and W. G. Bell (1921) even doubted it held prisoners at all. Other London prisons, such as Bridewell, had their own 'Little Ease'.
floors.visual: A tiny, pitch-dark stone cell in the vaults beneath the White Tower, closed by a heavy door with no window or air vent, and too cramped to stand or lie full length. Its exact dimensions and location are unknown.

floors.title: The Blood Countess
floors.claim: Witnesses at the 1611 trial of Elizabeth Báthory's servants said she bathed in young women's blood to stay young.
floors.answer: The 1611 witnesses accused her of torture and murder, but not blood baths. That story first appears in print around 1729.
floors.explanation: Elizabeth Báthory was arrested at Čachtice at the end of December 1610 and held there until she died in August 1614. Servants' testimony accused her of beating, burning and torturing young women. None of it mentions bathing in blood. The blood-bath story first appears in print about 1729, in the Jesuit László Turóczi's Tragica Historia, more than a century after her death. The Polish historian Adam Szabelski notes that while the case was being prepared, no one accused her of anything like it. When the witness statements were published in 1817, they showed the bathing tale was legend. The killings she was accused of are on record. The blood baths are not.
floors.nuance: This floor tests only the blood-bath story, not whether she was guilty, which historians still argue about. Szabelski, who argues she was the victim of a political plot, is cited only for where the legend came from. Her confinement is also disputed: the palatine Thurzó wrote that she was locked in a bricked-up room, but church visit records from July 1614 suggest she could move about the castle, so the claim avoids 'walled up alive'. Her arrest is dated 29 December, 30 December or New Year's Eve 1610.
floors.visual: A hilltop castle in western Slovakia, now a ruin. Sources do not describe the rooms she was kept in. Thurzó's 'bricked room' contradicts later visit records, so the space is unknown.

sources.title: Postać Elżbiety Batory w historiografii (The Figure of Elisabeth Bathory in Historiography)
sources.publisher: Studia Europaea Gnesnensia 9 (2014), Adam Mickiewicz University, DOI 10.14746/SEG.2014.9.6
sources.author: Adam Szabelski

sources.title: The Blood Countess: 10 Facts About Elizabeth Báthory
sources.author: Léonie Chao-Fong

sources.title: Elizabeth Báthory

floors.title: The Pendle witches' gaol
floors.claim: Old Demdike, one of the accused Pendle witches, died in Lancaster Castle before she could be tried.
floors.answer: She died in Lancaster Castle while waiting for the August 1612 trials.
floors.explanation: In spring 1612 Elizabeth Southerns, known as Old Demdike, and others from the Pendle area were sent to Lancaster gaol to wait for the August assizes. The trials ran from 18 to 19 August 1612, and ten of the condemned were hanged on the moor above the town on 20 August. Demdike was never tried. Lancaster Castle's own history says the 80-year-old 'had died in prison at Lancaster Castle whilst awaiting trial'. The historian Robert Poole likewise records that of those imprisoned, one died in gaol. Thomas Potts, the court clerk, printed the official account of the trials in 1613.
floors.nuance: Tradition, repeated by the castle itself, says the accused were held in a dungeon below the Well Tower (also called the Witches' Tower). No document from 1612 names the cell, so the claim leaves the Well Tower out. The date of Demdike's death is not recorded. Potts's 1613 account is the original record of the trials, but its text could not be checked for this page, so it is not quoted or cited.
floors.visual: Lancaster Castle's own pages say the accused were held in 'the same dungeon below the Well Tower', an underground space. That rests on tradition, and no size or layout is given.

sources.title: Lancashire Witch Trials
sources.supports: Says Old Demdike, aged 80, died in prison at Lancaster Castle while awaiting trial, and that the August 1612 assize trial lasted three days.

sources.title: The Pendle Witches
sources.supports: Says the accused were held in Lancaster Castle awaiting the August Assize, the trials began on 18 August 1612, the most famous of the witches died before trial, and ten were hanged on 20 August 1612.

sources.title: The Lancashire Witches 1612–2012
sources.author: Robert Poole
sources.supports: Independent scholar's account: Demdike was sent to Lancaster gaol in early April to await trial, and of those imprisoned at the castle one died in gaol.

sources.title: The Pendle Witches

floors.title: The fallen finance minister
floors.claim: Nicolas Fouquet, Louis XIV's disgraced finance minister, left Pignerol alive and became the Man in the Iron Mask.
floors.answer: Fouquet died at Pignerol in 1680. The masked prisoner died in the Bastille 23 years later.
floors.explanation: Fouquet was arrested in September 1661. On 20 December 1664 the court sentenced him to banishment, and Louis XIV personally changed that to life imprisonment. He was taken to the Alpine fortress of Pignerol, guarded by Saint-Mars, and held there in strict confinement for about fifteen years. Official records give his death at Pignerol on 23 March 1680. The masked prisoner died in the Bastille on 19 November 1703, twenty-three years later. Fouquet has been put forward as the masked man, but the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica says he 'undoubtedly died at Pignerol in 1680' and that 'the facts are a sufficient refutation' of the idea. There is a real link: the leading candidate, Eustache Dauger, served as one of Fouquet's valets in prison.
floors.nuance: No death certificate was drawn up, and that gap keeps the survival theories going. The official record is still treated as reliable. Larousse says sixteen years and Wikipedia says fifteen. The difference depends on whether the count starts at his transfer in December 1664.
floors.visual: A walled citadel above Pinerolo in the Alps. None of the sources checked describe Fouquet's rooms, so the interior is unknown.

sources.title: Iron Mask (1911 Encyclopædia Britannica)
sources.author: Hugh Chisholm
sources.supports: Says Fouquet 'undoubtedly died at Pignerol in 1680', lists him among the proposed identities and rejects him, and gives Saint-Mars's command of Pignerol, late 1664 to 1681.

sources.title: Fouquet (Nicolas)
sources.supports: Gives the 20 December 1664 sentence of banishment, changed by the king to life imprisonment, his confinement in the Pignerol fortress, and his death at Pignerol in 1680.

sources.title: Nicolas Fouquet
sources.supports: Says he was taken to Pignerol in December 1664, that official records give his death there on 23 March 1680, and that no death certificate was made.

floors.site: The Man in the Iron Mask (Pignerol, Exilles, Sainte-Marguerite, Bastille)
floors.title: Iron or velvet?
floors.claim: The Man in the Iron Mask's face was hidden behind a mask made of iron.
floors.answer: The Bastille's own officer wrote down a black velvet mask. The iron came later, from legend and Voltaire.
floors.explanation: The prisoner was moved with his jailer Saint-Mars from Pignerol to Exilles (1681), to the island of Sainte-Marguerite (1687), and finally to the Bastille in September 1698. Étienne du Junca, the king's lieutenant at the Bastille, kept a journal of eyewitness entries. On 19 November 1703 he recorded the death of 'the unknown prisoner, always masked with a black velvet mask'. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica finds no evidence that the mask was anything but black velvet, and says that 'only afterwards' did legend turn it into iron. Voltaire did most to spread the story, in Le Siècle de Louis XIV (1751) and later writings. The French history site Hérodote puts it plainly: 'un masque de velours noir (et non de fer)'.
floors.nuance: The prisoner and the mask are both on record. Only the iron is myth. Who the prisoner was is still unsettled. Eustache Dauger is the leading candidate, and the 1911 Britannica also discusses Mattioli. The burial name appears as 'Marchioly' and 'Marchiali'.
floors.visual: A prisoner whose face is covered by a black velvet mask. The rooms in the Bastille and in the earlier fortresses are not described in the sources checked.

sources.title: Iron Mask (1911 Encyclopædia Britannica)
sources.author: Hugh Chisholm
sources.supports: Quotes du Junca's 1703 entry ('always masked with a black velvet mask'), says the iron came later from legend, gives Voltaire's role, and gives Saint-Mars's moves from Pignerol to Exilles, Sainte-Marguerite and the Bastille.

sources.title: 19 novembre 1703 : mort du Masque de fer
sources.author: Camille Vignolle
sources.supports: Says the mask was 'de velours noir (et non de fer)', gives the route Pignerol (to 1681), Exilles (to 1687), Sainte-Marguerite (to 1698), Bastille, and the death on 19 November 1703.

sources.title: Man in the Iron Mask
sources.supports: Quotes du Junca's 'mask of black velvet', says Voltaire later misreported it as iron, and records Saint-Mars taking up the Bastille post on 18 September 1698.

floors.title: The Whigs' Vault
floors.claim: In 1685 about 167 Covenanter men and women were packed into a single vault at Dunnottar Castle.
floors.answer: About 167 men and women were held in one cellar for some two months in 1685.
floors.explanation: In 1685, with a rising feared in the south of Scotland, Covenanters held in Edinburgh were marched north to Dunnottar. In May, 167 prisoners, 122 men and 45 women, were locked into a cellar below one of the buildings in the courtyard. It became known as the Whigs' Vault. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica records 'no fewer than 167' held in that dungeon, and the castle's own history gives the same total. They were held for about two months with little fresh air and no facilities. Some died of starvation and disease, and others were killed trying to escape. Most survivors were then shipped to the colonies as forced labour.
floors.nuance: The total of 167 is consistent across sources, but the split varies: 122 men and 45 women in Undiscovered Scotland, 47 women on covenanter.org.uk, and 112 men on a transcribed site plaque. Death counts vary and are left out. 'About 167' allows for that. The castle's site says 'over 167'.
floors.visual: A single vaulted cellar beneath one of the buildings in the courtyard of a cliff-top castle, with little fresh air and no facilities. Sources checked give no dimensions or window details.

sources.title: Dunnottar Castle (1911 Encyclopædia Britannica)
sources.supports: 'In 1685 the castle was converted into a Covenanters' prison … no fewer than 167 being confined in a dungeon, called therefrom the Whigs' Vault.'

sources.title: History
sources.supports: The castle's own history: in 1685 over 167 Covenanters and Whigs were imprisoned in a cellar in terrible conditions.

sources.title: Dunnottar Castle Feature Page
sources.supports: Gives May 1685, 167 prisoners (122 men, 45 women), the vault below a building in the Quadrangle, about two months' confinement, deaths from starvation, disease and escape attempts, and transportation.

sources.title: Dunnottar Castle
sources.supports: Says prisoners were moved from Edinburgh because a rebellion was feared, describes a single room with little fresh air and no facilities, and says most were banished to the Americas.

floors.title: The tsar's son
floors.claim: Peter the Great's son and heir, Alexei, died a prisoner in St Petersburg's fortress in 1718, two days after a flogging with the knout.
floors.answer: Alexei died in the fortress on 26 June 1718 (Old Style), two days after his last flogging; exactly how is still debated.
floors.explanation: Tsarevich Alexei fled abroad, was lured home, and was forced to 'confess', which implicated his friends. In June 1718 he was held in the guardhouse of the St Petersburg citadel, the Peter and Paul Fortress. On 19 June he received 25 strokes of the knout, a heavy whip, and on 24 June fifteen more. A court of 127 senators and officials sentenced him to death for treason. He died in the fortress on 26 June 1718 (Old Style; 7 July by the modern calendar). The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes that 'the natural inference is that he was not intended to survive' the flogging.
floors.nuance: Exactly how he died is not settled: the official account blamed illness, and some writers argue he was killed in secret. The claim keeps to what all sources agree on: place, year, and the flogging two days before. Dates are Old Style.
floors.visual: A guardhouse inside the walled island fortress on the Neva. Sources checked do not describe his cell. The famous Trubetskoy Bastion prison was built only in 1870–72, so it should not be drawn.

sources.title: Alexius Petrovich (1911 Encyclopædia Britannica)
sources.supports: Gives the 25 knout strokes on 19 June and 15 on 24 June, the senate's death sentence, confinement 'in the guardhouse of the citadel of St Petersburg', and death two days after the last flogging.

sources.title: Peter the Great Tortured and Killed His Own Son
sources.author: Jesse Greenspan
sources.supports: Says he was whipped 25 times on 19 June 1718, tortured again five days later, and died of his wounds on 26 June (7 July New Style).

sources.title: Alexei Petrovich, Tsarevich of Russia
sources.supports: Gives his death on 26 June (O.S.) 1718 in the Peter and Paul Fortress, the 127-member court's death sentence on 24 June, and the knout floggings.

floors.title: Oglethorpe's gaols committee
floors.claim: After Oglethorpe's 1729 inquiry exposed the Marshalsea, its warden William Acton was convicted of murdering a prisoner.
floors.answer: The inquiry exposed terrible conditions, and Acton was tried for four murders, but he was acquitted every time.
floors.explanation: In 1729 a House of Commons committee chaired by James Oglethorpe inspected the Marshalsea. Its report describes over 330 poor debtors on the 'common side', with 32 to 40 people locked overnight in a room about 16 by 14 feet, some in hammocks above others. In the spring 'not less than Eight or Ten usually died every 24 Hours'. The Commons asked the King to have the Attorney-General prosecute the wardens William Acton and John Darby. Acton was tried at Kingston for the murders of Thomas Bliss, Captain John Bromfield, Robert Newton and James Thompson, and was acquitted each time. The suffering is on record. The conviction never happened.
floors.nuance: Sources disagree on the date of the Bliss trial: All the Year Round (1867) gives 6 July 1729 and a printed trial account reportedly gives 1 August 1729. The claim avoids a date. The 'Eight or Ten' a day figure is the report's description of the worst period, before the committee's intervention.
floors.visual: A brick-walled common side for poor debtors. In George's Ward, 32 to 40 people were locked overnight in a room about 16 by 14 feet, some slung in hammocks above those on the floor. A damp, uncovered 'Strong Room' was used for punishment.

sources.title: A Report from the Committee appointed to Enquire into the State of the Goals of this Kingdom: Relating to the Marshalsea Prison (1729), ch. 14 in The Publications of James Edward Oglethorpe
sources.author: James Edward Oglethorpe (committee report)
sources.supports: The report text and editor's note give the overcrowding and death figures, the Commons resolution to prosecute Acton and Darby, and that Acton was tried for four murders and 'found innocent in each trial'.

sources.title: All the Year Round, vol. XVIII, p. 252
sources.supports: Says Acton was tried for the murder of Bliss at the Kingston assizes and acquitted, and that other charges also ended in acquittal. Also describes the Strong Room.

floors.site: Newgate Prison and the Old Bailey
floors.title: The Black Assize
floors.claim: In 1750 gaol fever carried from Newgate into the Old Bailey courtroom killed the Lord Mayor of London.
floors.answer: Gaol fever from Newgate killed the Lord Mayor, two judges and many others at the 1750 sessions.
floors.explanation: Newgate was so overcrowded and filthy that 'gaol fever', a typhus-type disease, was always present. At the spring 1750 sessions in the courthouse next door, prisoners brought the infection into court on their bodies and clothes. John Noorthouck's 1773 History of London names the dead: Lord Mayor Sir Samuel Pennant, Alderman Sir Daniel Lambert, Baron Clarke of the Exchequer, Judge Abney of the Common Pleas, the under-sheriff, most of the Middlesex jury and several spectators. The architectural historian Harold Kalman puts the toll at sixty. Afterwards Newgate was cleaned and fitted with ventilators. Seven of the eleven workmen who installed them caught the fever, and one died.
floors.nuance: Noorthouck says the May 1750 sessions and Kalman says April 1750, so the claim gives only the year. The total varies: Noorthouck gives no number and Kalman says sixty. Linking gaol fever to typhus is the modern identification.
floors.visual: An overcrowded, filthy gaol with foul air, next door to the sessions house where crowded courtroom audiences sat close to the prisoners.

sources.title: A New History of London Including Westminster and Southwark, Book 1, ch. 21: 1745–1755
sources.author: John Noorthouck
sources.supports: Names the dead of the May 1750 Old Bailey sessions (Pennant, Lambert, Clarke, Abney, Cox, most of the jury), traces the infection to overcrowded Newgate, and records the ventilators installed afterwards.

sources.title: Newgate Prison
sources.author: Harold D. Kalman
sources.supports: Says the fever spread to the adjoining sessions house in April 1750, that sixty died including the Lord Mayor, two judges and an alderman, and that seven of eleven ventilator workmen caught it.

floors.site: Magdeburg fortress (the Star Fort, or Sternschanze)
floors.title: The prisoner in 68 pounds of iron
floors.claim: Friedrich von der Trenck spent almost ten years in Magdeburg's fortress, most of them chained to the wall of his cell.
floors.answer: He was held for nearly ten years and chained to the wall after his escape attempts.
floors.explanation: Trenck was a Prussian officer who had fallen out with Frederick the Great. He was arrested in Danzig and held at Magdeburg for close to ten years, until he was freed in 1763 after Empress Maria Theresa stepped in. The German national biography (1894) says he was chained to the wall so that he could not escape. The Victoria and Albert Museum holds a pewter cup that Trenck engraved in prison in October 1763. One of its scenes shows him chained to a wall by a neck collar and chain marked '68 lbs.' In his memoirs (1787; English edition 1788) he describes a neck collar, an iron belt, a bar between his wrists and a heavy staple in the wall. Historians accept the imprisonment and the chaining.
floors.nuance: He was put in chains after his escape attempts, not on arrival, so the chaining covers most of his stay rather than all of it. The 68-pound (about 31 kg) figure is Trenck's own, on the cup he engraved in 1763 and again in his memoirs. No independent record of the weight was found. Accounts give his arrest as 1753 or 1754; Penkert says 1754. The V&A gives his time at Magdeburg as 'nine years, five months and some days'. The memoirs say the arm irons were taken off a month after they were first put on, when he fell ill.
floors.visual: A small cell in a casemate (a vaulted room inside the fortress walls), shut by several doors. The 1788 plate shows Trenck in an iron neck collar with chains hanging from it, an iron belt riveted round his body and a two-foot bar between his handcuffs. Everything is fixed to a thick iron staple in the wall, with a brick seat under the staple, a water jug, and a gravestone carved TRENCK at his feet.

sources.title: Trenckbecher (beaker and lid), museum no. M.148-1930
sources.supports: Trenck engraved the cup at Magdeburg in October 1763 while still a prisoner; he was confined there 'nine years, five months and some days', was chained to the wall, and one scene marks his collar and chain '68 lbs'.

sources.supports: The frontispiece caption reads 'loaded with 68 pounds weight of irons in the dungeon of Magdeburg', and the explanation of the plate describes the collar, belt, bar and wall staple.

floors.title: Counting the Black Hole
floors.claim: On one night in 1756, 146 prisoners were crammed into Calcutta's 'Black Hole', and 123 of them suffocated.
floors.answer: Many died that night, but the 146 and 123 come from one survivor's pamphlet, and historians think far fewer were inside.
floors.explanation: Something terrible did happen. After the Nawab of Bengal's forces took Fort William, British prisoners spent the night of 20 June 1756 locked in the fort's small punishment cell, and many died. The famous figures, though, come from one survivor, John Zephaniah Holwell, whose 1758 pamphlet says 123 of 146 prisoners smothered. Holwell himself put the room at about 18 feet square, and from 1896 critics argued that 146 people could not fit in it. In a 1959 study, the historian Brijen Gupta noted that Indian scholars had come to accept Jadunath Sarkar's view that 'probably not more than sixty' were confined. Gupta named twenty-one survivors. Most historians accept that the event happened but treat Holwell's numbers as greatly exaggerated.
floors.nuance: The verdict is on the 146 and 123 figures, not on whether the event happened. In 1915–16 J. H. Little called the whole story a 'gigantic hoax'; most later historians do not go that far. Estimates of the true numbers vary. The often-quoted 64 confined and 21 survivors is credited to Gupta by some writers and to Wolpert or Prior by others; the part of Gupta's article that is freely readable does not give the 64. Holwell gives the room as a cube of about 18 feet; other accounts give 14 by 18 feet.
floors.visual: In Holwell's words, a 'cube of about eighteen feet': closed by solid walls to the east and south, a wall and door to the north, and open only to the west through two small windows 'strongly barred with iron', on a close, sultry night.

sources.title: A Genuine Narrative of the Deplorable Deaths of the English Gentlemen, and Others, who were Suffocated in the Black-Hole (archive.org scan)
sources.author: J. Z. Holwell
sources.supports: The source of the figures ('of one hundred and forty-six prisoners, one hundred and twenty-three were smothered'), the date (night of 20 June 1756) and the room ('a cube of about eighteen feet', two barred windows).

sources.title: The Black Hole Incident (Journal of Asian Studies 19:1, pp. 53–63)
sources.publisher: Cambridge University Press / Association for Asian Studies
sources.author: Brijen K. Gupta
sources.supports: Records the dispute over Holwell's count of 123 dead, cites Jadunath Sarkar's view that 'probably not more than sixty were confined', and names twenty-one survivors.

sources.title: History and Myth out of Calcutta
sources.publisher: UCLA Center for India and South Asia
sources.supports: Holwell's account is the main source and others are hard to find; Bholanath Chunder argued in 1896 that 146 people could not fit; J. H. Little in 1916 called the story a 'giant hoax'.

sources.title: Black Hole of Calcutta
sources.supports: Gives the date (night of 20 June 1756), the 14 by 18 feet room, and lower modern estimates (for example 64 confined and 21 survivors).

floors.title: Casanova over the rooftops
floors.claim: Giacomo Casanova really escaped from the Piombi prison by breaking out onto the lead roof of the Doge's Palace.
floors.answer: Venice's own records punish the jailer for the escape and pay for repairing the hole they broke out through.
floors.explanation: Casanova was locked in the Piombi, the cells under the Doge's Palace's lead roof, in 1755 and sentenced to five years. On the night of 31 October 1756 he and a fellow prisoner, the monk Marino Balbi, broke through the ceiling and out onto the sloping roof. They climbed back in through a dormer window and walked out of the palace at dawn. The detailed story is Casanova's own, written in 1787. Venice's own records back up the core of it, though. A note by the State Inquisitors dated 10 June 1757 punishes the jailer for the 'flight, on the first of November last, from the Piombi' of Balbi and Casanova. A repair bill also lists the cost of sealing 'the hole where they fled'.
floors.nuance: Only Casanova describes the route over the roof and through the palace. Some 19th- and 20th-century critics, Rinaldo Fulin among them, argued that the Inquisitors or his friends had quietly helped him. The archivist Charles Samaran (1922) says none of them produced firm proof. The night began on 31 October (the date of the farewell note Casanova left) and the official record dates the flight to 1 November. The cells shown to visitors today are reconstructions.
floors.visual: Six or seven cells made by dividing the palace attic with wooden partitions, thickly studded with nails and strengthened with iron plates, directly under a steep roof covered in lead sheets (piombi). Casanova's two cells have been rebuilt and are on the museum's Secret Itineraries tour.

sources.title: Histoire de ma fuite des prisons de la République de Venise qu'on appelle les Plombs, introduction and notes by Charles Samaran (archive.org scan)
sources.author: Giacomo Casanova; ed. Charles Samaran
sources.supports: Contains Casanova's account of the roof escape and his note dated 31 October 1756. Samaran's notes quote the Inquisitors' annotation of 10 June 1757 dating the flight of Balbi and Casanova from the Piombi to 1 November, and a repair bill for 'il foro dove è fugiti'.

sources.title: Itinerari segreti di Palazzo Ducale (visitor booklet)
sources.supports: The Piombi were six or seven attic cells under the lead roof with nailed, iron-plated wooden partitions; Casanova was held there and described them; his first and second cells are on the tour.

sources.title: Special itineraries
sources.publisher: Palazzo Ducale, Fondazione Musei Civici di Venezia
sources.supports: The Piombi held Council of Ten prisoners, take their name from the lead roof, and Casanova's rebuilt cells are part of the tour.

sources.title: Giacomo Casanova
sources.supports: Arrested 26 July 1755, sentenced to five years on 12 September; with Balbi he broke through to the roof, re-entered by a dormer window and left the palace by gondola.

floors.title: Mirabeau, not Monte Cristo
floors.claim: The Château d'If, made famous by Dumas's Count of Monte Cristo, really held the young Count of Mirabeau, locked up in 1774 by royal order.
floors.answer: Mirabeau was held there for some months from 1774 on a royal order. Dantès and Faria are fiction.
floors.explanation: Edmond Dantès and the Abbé Faria are characters in Dumas's serial novel. The French Ministry of Culture's heritage record says Dumas placed their cells in the fort 'in a fictional way'. The fort did hold real prisoners, though, among them hundreds of Protestants, revolutionaries and the future revolutionary leader Mirabeau. The Centre des monuments nationaux, which runs the site, says Mirabeau was held there for a few months. Provence's tourism publication dates his arrival to 1774 and says he was held under a lettre de cachet, a royal order allowing imprisonment without trial. It was obtained by his father to punish his debts and wild living. The 'Dantès' and 'Faria' cells came later: their names were painted over the doors to keep the legend alive.
floors.nuance: That his father asked for the order comes from the French historian Roger Duchêne (Le château d'If et les îles, 1996), as cited by French Wikipedia. His stay is usually dated 1774–1775. The real priest José Custódio de Faria is said to have inspired Dumas, but none of the sources checked for this page shows he was ever held at If. The hole between the two 'show' cells was dug by a guard, and the Dantès cell is a reconstruction for tourists. Sources differ on when visitors were first shown it: 1844 or 1848.
floors.visual: A square three-storey fort with round towers on a bare limestone island. The poorest prisoners were kept in dark, damp cells at the base of the towers ('culs de tour') or in crowded shared rooms on the ground floor. Paying prisoners had single rooms ('pistoles') in former officers' quarters on the first floor.

sources.title: Histoire du château d'If
sources.supports: Mirabeau was 'interné quelques mois'; describes the 'culs de tour', the shared ground-floor rooms and the paid 'pistoles'; mentions Dantès and Faria as Dumas's characters.

sources.title: Château d'If (Mérimée notice PA00081333)
sources.supports: It was a prison for centuries that held Mirabeau and Cadoudal, and Dumas placed the cells of Dantès and Faria there fictionally.

sources.title: Le château d'If, entre mythe et réalité
sources.author: Virginie d'Humières

sources.title: Château d'If (site guide)
sources.supports: 'Mirabeau enfermé en 1774 sur lettre de cachet'.

sources.title: Château d'If

floors.title: The 'iron' cage made of wood
floors.claim: Mont-Saint-Michel's notorious prison cage, the 'iron cage' blamed on Louis XI, was made of iron.
floors.answer: Louis-Philippe, who saw it as a boy, remembered it as made of great pieces of wood, and the architect Corroyer, who studied the abbey, wrote in 1877 that it was wood.
floors.explanation: The abbey held state prisoners from the late Middle Ages until 1863, and its most feared object was a cage. Legend called it Louis XI's 'iron cage'. The Manche departmental archives describe the iron cage as famous 'but legendary'. Two people who saw the real thing say otherwise. Édouard Corroyer, the government architect who studied the abbey, wrote in 1877 that the 'famous cage, called iron, was in fact of wood'. The future King Louis-Philippe saw it as a boy and remembered it in his memoirs as 'made of great pieces of wood', standing in a horrible, damp cell. The prior told him it was hardly ever used, only for a day or two as a special punishment. A gazetteer (newspaper writer) known as Dubourg was held in it in 1745, Corroyer says.
floors.nuance: The legend speaks of a cage of wood and iron, and it may well have had iron fittings; the myth is that it was an iron cage. Sources disagree on how it ended. The architect Corroyer says it was destroyed in 1777 during a visit by the Count of Artois. Louis-Philippe, who saw it as a boy, says only its door was taken off during his visit; the year of that visit is uncertain (the school anthology that reprints his account dates it to 1777, which seems too early, since he was born in 1773). The tale the monks told him, that a writer spent seventeen years in it for mocking Louis XIV, is not confirmed. The cage shown today is a reconstruction.
floors.visual: A cage built of thick wooden beams inside a dark, damp vaulted cell of the abbey. French Wikipedia says that, according to legend, it hung beneath a vault. One post had a flower scratched into it with a nail by a prisoner.

sources.title: Description de l'abbaye du Mont Saint-Michel et de ses abords (archive.org scan)

floors.title: Seven prisoners
floors.claim: When crowds stormed the Bastille on 14 July 1789, the great royal prison held just seven prisoners.
floors.answer: Four forgers, two men judged mad and one count: seven prisoners in all.
floors.explanation: The fortress-prison that stood for royal tyranny was almost empty when it fell. Four of its prisoners were forgers (Béchade, Laroche, La Corrège and Pujade), held over a forged bill of exchange. Two men were considered mad: Tavernier, and an Irish-born man named Whyte, or de Whyte. The seventh was the Comte de Solages, locked up at his family's request for sexual misconduct. The Marquis de Sade, its most famous recent inmate, had been moved out about ten days earlier after shouting to people in the street that prisoners were being murdered. The crowd mainly wanted the gunpowder stored there, and it freed all seven.
floors.nuance: Sources describe Tavernier differently. Some call him mentally ill, others a man linked to a plot against Louis XV some thirty years earlier. The count of seven and the split of four forgers, two 'madmen' and one nobleman are not in dispute. Sade was moved to the Charenton asylum in early July 1789.
floors.visual: A massive fortress with eight towers joined by curtain walls, about 24 m (78 ft) high and 3 m thick at the base, surrounded by water-filled ditches. Most prisoners lived in eight-sided tower rooms with a stove or fireplace, simple furniture and usually a window. The rooms under the roofs were the worst, and the underground cells were hardly used by then.

sources.title: Le Guichet du Savoir: question on the prisoners of the Bastille in 1789

floors.title: The maiden who never killed
floors.claim: The Iron Maiden of Nuremberg was a medieval torture device used to execute prisoners.
floors.answer: No medieval use is recorded. The story appears in the 1790s, and the cabinets shown were assembled in the 1800s.
floors.explanation: No medieval record of an iron maiden being used has been found. The story first appears at the end of the 18th century. Johann Philipp Siebenkees, a professor at Altdorf, published it in 1793, claiming a coin forger was executed in one in Nuremberg on 14 August 1515. Historians doubt it: no record of such an execution has been found, and he probably invented or embroidered the tale. The spiked cabinets shown in the 19th century were put together for display. Wolfgang Schild, a historian of criminal law, argued that they were assembled from museum objects and reworked from early-modern 'shame cloaks', which were barrels or mantles worn as a public humiliation punishment. The Medieval Crime Museum in Rothenburg owns a 19th-century copy of the Nuremberg maiden. Its own label says the device was used for shame punishments, not torture or killing, and that 'the dangerous nails were added later'.
floors.nuance: The 1793 date is as reported by German Wikipedia, citing Der Spiegel (2022); the medievalist Peter Konieczny dates the story's first appearance to the end of the 18th century, in a Nuremberg guidebook by Siebenkees, and also gives the 1515 tale. German Wikipedia links Siebenkees's account to a 1533 chronicle entry, so he may have embroidered an older story rather than inventing one. The Nuremberg original was destroyed in Allied bombing in 1944 or 1945. An execution in 1515 would in any case be early modern rather than medieval. Because the legend dates from 1793, this floor comes after the Bastille.
floors.visual: A tall, hinged iron cabinet shaped roughly like a woman or a mummy case, with doors lined inside with spikes. The Rothenburg piece is a 19th-century copy of the Nuremberg maiden, and the museum says its nails were added later.

sources.title: Medieval Crime Museum
sources.supports: 'Iron Maiden: no torture!': it was not used for torture or murder but for shame punishments, and 'the dangerous nails were added later'.

sources.title: Medieval torture devices

floors.site: The oubliette (castles everywhere; Warwick Castle as the example)
floors.place: Warwick Castle, England, and castles across Europe
floors.years: medieval castles; myth popular in the 1800s
floors.title: The myth that invented the dungeon
floors.claim: Medieval castles commonly had oubliettes: pits where prisoners were dropped through a trapdoor and left to be forgotten.
floors.answer: True forgetting pits were rare; many supposed oubliettes were really storerooms, latrines or ice stores.
floors.explanation: Castles did hold prisoners, but purpose-built 'forgetting pits' were rare. Even Viollet-le-Duc, whose 19th-century dictionary gave the oubliette its classic illustrated description, complained that every medieval castle showed visitors an oubliette when real examples were 'very rarely' found. He knew of only three cases that could reasonably be called oubliettes, and of those he thought Chinon's was probably a latrine and the Bastille's could pass for an ice store. He quoted the writer and monuments inspector Prosper Mérimée, who warned that the Middle Ages were too often painted 'in atrocious colours'. Modern historians agree that many 'dungeons' and 'oubliettes' were storerooms, cellars, ice chambers, cisterns or latrines. The famous pit at Warwick Castle is more likely a latrine. The dread of the oubliette owes more to Romantic novels, such as Walter Scott's Ivanhoe (1819), than to medieval practice.
floors.nuance: Viollet-le-Duc was more sceptic than promoter: his dictionary fixed the popular image, but of his three plausible cases he accepted only Pierrefonds without reservation. The word itself is medieval French; what came later was the belief that oubliettes were everywhere. Leap Castle's story of 'three cartloads of bones' is left out because it traces only to popular and tourist accounts, not to a documented find. Chris Bishop's 2019 study of the dungeon in popular imagination is behind a paywall; it is cited for its subject, not for a specific quotation.
floors.visual: The legend pictures a narrow shaft under a trapdoor in a vaulted floor, dropping into a dark pit. Viollet-le-Duc's 'Bastille oubliette' was a vaulted six-sided chamber with an inverted cone at its centre, probably an ice store. Warwick's supposed oubliette is a short shaft under an iron grille that opens into a larger chamber.
